title: Capstone: A Question, Evidence and Your Argument
bigQuestion: How do you build an argument that is honest about the evidence and fair to the people who disagree with you?

story.title: The Answer Maya Thought She Knew
story.kicker: A student starts her capstone sure of her answer, and the evidence sends her somewhere new.
paragraphs: Maya chose her capstone question in five minutes: What best helps people move up in life? She already knew the answer. Go to college. Her older cousin had been the first in the family to finish a degree, and now he worked as an engineer. Maya planned to find three studies that agreed with her and be done by Friday.

The first surprise came from Germany. Maya read that many Germans reach steady, well-paid work through apprenticeships, not university. The second came from a set of numbers. Economists had compared how much parents' income predicts their children's income in different countries. Denmark and Canada showed much more movement between generations than the United States. Yet Americans attend college at high rates.

The third surprise was closer to home. A team led by economist Raj Chetty had found that children's chances of moving up varied widely across American cities and counties. Where a child grew up seemed to matter, not only whether they went to college. Maya started a new page in her notebook. At the top she wrote: Maybe college is one road, not the only one.

She found strong arguments she had never considered. Some writers on the left pointed to public schools, health care and support for poor families. Some writers on the right pointed to stable families, strong local communities, work and economic growth. Maya noticed that both sides had evidence. Neither side had all of it.

On Friday Maya was not done. She had a better question, a messier answer and twice as many sources. Her teacher read the new page and nodded. You changed your mind because of evidence, she said. That is what this project is for.
story.think: Why is changing your mind because of evidence a strength and not a failure, and what evidence would it take to change yours on a question you care about?

lessons.title: Choosing a Strong Question
lessons.mainIdea: A strong capstone question is open, arguable and researchable, so reasonable people could answer it differently using evidence.
reading: Compare two questions. When did the Berlin Wall fall? The answer is 1989, and it is settled. Why do some democracies last while others collapse? Historians and political scientists still argue about that one. The first is a fact question. The second is a *research question*: open, worth arguing, and answerable with evidence rather than opinion alone.

This course suggests three kinds of capstone questions. What best helps people move up? Why do some democracies last? What makes an ideology turn extreme? Each has a record to study. The last question, for example, can draw on the Nazi regime and the Holocaust, and on Communist regimes such as the Soviet Gulag system and the Khmer Rouge in Cambodia, where about a quarter of the population died between 1975 and 1979.

A good question is also narrow enough to finish. What causes poverty in the world? is too big for a semester. What helped South Korea move from poverty to wealth after the 1950s, compared with Mexico? is a better *scope*. Finally, a good question has more than one serious answer. If only one answer is possible, you do not have an *arguable claim* to make.

words.d: an open question that can be answered with evidence and on which reasonable people might disagree
how wide or narrow a question is; how much ground it tries to cover
a statement that some informed people could reasonably dispute, which you must support with evidence

look.title: Sort the Questions
look.text: 1. In what year did Mexico adopt its current constitution? 2. Is Japan a good country? 3. Why did Weimar Germany's democracy collapse by 1933 while Britain's survived the same Great Depression? 4. How can we solve every problem of inequality on Earth?
look.prompt: Which question makes the best capstone question, and what is wrong with each of the others?

check.q: Which is a research question rather than a fact question?
choices: When did the Berlin Wall fall?
What is the capital of Japan?
Why do some democracies last while others collapse?
How many states does Germany have?
check.why: It is open and arguable; experts still disagree about the answer.

check.q: Why is What causes poverty in the world? a weak capstone question?
choices: Its scope is too big to finish well
It has no evidence at all
It is only about one person
check.why: The reading says the question is too big for a semester, so its scope needs narrowing.

check.q: What makes a claim arguable?
choices: It is a personal feeling no one can check
It is a date everyone agrees on
It is copied from one source
Some informed people could reasonably dispute it
check.why: An arguable claim can be reasonably disputed and must be supported with evidence.

lessons.title: Gathering Evidence From Two Regions
lessons.mainIdea: Evidence from at least two regions lets you test whether a pattern is general or only true in one place.
reading: Suppose your question is what helps people move up. If you study only the United States, you cannot tell whether your answer is about human societies or only about one country. Adding Germany, Japan, Mexico or Denmark lets you compare. This method is called *comparative analysis*: studying cases side by side to see which causes seem to matter.

Sources come in two main kinds. A *primary source* comes from the time or people being studied: a constitution, a census table, a speech or a survey. A *secondary source* is written later by someone interpreting the evidence, like a history book or a research article. Strong projects use both. Primary sources give you the raw record. Secondary sources show how experts have read it.

Check every source. Who made it, and why? Is it published by a known body, such as the OECD, the World Bank, a national statistics office or a university press? Does another source agree? This habit is called *corroboration*. A single striking number shared on social media, with no author or date, is not yet evidence. Find where it came from before you use it.

words.d: studying two or more cases side by side to see which causes or features seem to matter
evidence created by the people or at the time being studied, such as a law, census or speech
a later account that interprets evidence, such as a history book or research article
checking whether other reliable sources agree with a piece of evidence

look.title: How Long to Climb the Ladder?
look.cite: OECD, A Broken Social Elevator? How to Promote Social Mobility, 2018, rounded
look.prompt: The OECD estimated how many generations it would take a child from a low-income family to reach average income. What does comparing five countries show that studying one country could not?

check.q: Which is a primary source?
choices: A blog post summarizing a study
A documentary made fifty years later
check.why: A census table is part of the original record, created at the time being studied.

check.q: Why does the reading recommend evidence from at least two regions?
choices: Because one country never has data
To test whether a pattern is general or only true in one place
check.why: Comparative analysis shows which causes seem to matter across places.

check.q: What is corroboration?
choices: Checking whether other reliable sources agree
Copying a source word for word
Choosing sources that match your view
check.why: Corroboration means confirming evidence with other trustworthy sources.

lessons.title: Reading Numbers Carefully
lessons.mainIdea: Numbers are powerful evidence only when you know what they measure, who measured them and what they cannot show.
reading: Economist Miles Corak compared rich countries using a measure called *intergenerational earnings elasticity*. It shows how strongly a father's earnings predict his son's. A figure near zero means children's earnings barely depend on their parents'. A figure near one means they depend almost entirely on them. In Corak's figures, Denmark scored about 0.15 and the United States about 0.47.

Countries with more income inequality also tended to show less mobility. Economist Alan Krueger named this pattern the Great Gatsby Curve in 2012. It is a *correlation*: two things that rise and fall together. A correlation does not prove that one thing causes the other. Inequality might block mobility, or a third factor, such as school quality or family structure, might drive both.

Read every number with questions. What exactly was measured, and for whom? Corak's data followed fathers and sons, partly because older records tracked men's earnings better. Figures from different studies can use different methods, so compare numbers from the same source when you can. Name the source every time. This is part of *data literacy*, the skill of reading numbers honestly.

words.d: a measure of how strongly parents' earnings predict their children's earnings; higher means less mobility
a pattern in which two things tend to rise or fall together, which does not by itself prove cause
when one thing actually produces a change in another
the skill of reading, questioning and explaining numbers honestly

look.title: How Much Do Fathers' Earnings Predict Sons'?
look.cite: Miles Corak, Income Inequality, Equality of Opportunity, and Intergenerational Mobility, Journal of Economic Perspectives, 2013
look.prompt: Which two countries show the least mobility between generations, and what is one reason you should be careful before saying why?

check.q: In Corak's figures, what does a higher elasticity mean?
choices: Children's earnings depend more on their parents'
check.why: Higher elasticity means parents' earnings predict children's more strongly, so there is less mobility.

check.q: What is the Great Gatsby Curve?
choices: A rule that proves inequality causes low mobility
A pattern linking higher inequality with lower mobility across countries
check.why: It is a correlation between inequality and lower mobility, named by Alan Krueger in 2012.

check.q: Why can't a correlation alone prove causation?
choices: A third factor might drive both things
Only one country can be studied at a time
check.why: Something like school quality could cause both patterns, so the link alone does not prove cause.

lessons.title: A Worked Case: Why Democracies Last
lessons.mainIdea: Scholars explain democratic survival with several factors, including wealth, strong institutions and leaders who accept the rules, and they still weigh these differently.
reading: Weimar Germany became a democracy in 1919. By 1933 Adolf Hitler was chancellor, and within months the democracy was gone. India became a democratic republic in 1950 while still very poor, and it has held regular elections since, with a break in civil rights during the Emergency of 1975 to 1977. Chile, one of Latin America's longest-running democracies, fell to a military coup in 1973 and returned to democracy in 1990. These cases make a good puzzle.

One well-known finding comes from political scientist Adam Przeworski and colleagues: democracies in richer countries have rarely collapsed. Wealth seems to help democracy survive once it exists. But India shows that a poor country can sustain democracy, and Weimar shows that a modern, educated country can lose it. So scholars also look at *institutions*, the rules and organizations like courts, parties and a free press.

In their 2018 book How Democracies Die, Steven Levitsky and Daniel Ziblatt argued that written rules are not enough. Democracies also depend on *norms*, unwritten habits. Two matter most, they said: *mutual toleration*, treating opponents as legitimate rivals rather than enemies, and forbearance, not using every legal power to the hilt. Other scholars stress economic crisis, war or outside pressure. A strong capstone weighs these explanations rather than picking one without evidence.

words.d: the rules and organizations that shape political life, such as courts, parties, elections and a free press
unwritten habits and expectations that guide how people use power
accepting political opponents as legitimate rivals who have a right to compete and govern
the sudden, illegal seizure of government power, often by the military

look.title: Guardrails of Democracy
look.text: Constitutions alone cannot protect a democracy. It also relies on two unwritten guardrails: rivals accepting each other as legitimate, and leaders holding back from using their full legal power to crush opponents.
look.cite: Steven Levitsky and Daniel Ziblatt, How Democracies Die, 2018 (paraphrased)
look.prompt: How could the idea of unwritten guardrails help explain why a democracy with a strong written constitution might still fail?

check.q: What does India's history add to the question of why democracies last?
choices: It shows that a poor country can sustain democracy
It proves only rich countries can be democracies
It shows that coups always succeed
It shows India never held elections
check.why: India has kept regular elections since 1950 while starting very poor, which complicates the wealth explanation.

check.q: According to Levitsky and Ziblatt, what are norms?
choices: Unwritten habits and expectations about how power is used
check.why: Norms are the unwritten guardrails, such as mutual toleration and forbearance.

check.q: What happened in Chile in 1973?
choices: Its democracy fell to a military coup
check.why: Chile's long-running democracy was overthrown by a military coup in 1973 and returned in 1990.

lessons.title: The Strongest Case From the Left
lessons.mainIdea: Thinkers on the left often argue that opportunity grows when government reduces inequality and invests in schools, health and families.
reading: Take Maya's question: what best helps people move up? Many on the political *left* start from the Nordic countries. Denmark and Norway combine high taxes with free university, strong public schools, paid parental leave and wide health coverage. They also show high mobility in Corak's figures. To left-leaning thinkers, that is no coincidence.

The argument runs like this. Children do not choose their parents. If a poor child lacks good schools, health care or a stable home, talent is wasted. Public spending evens the starting line, the argument goes, and *redistribution*, moving income from richer to poorer people through taxes and benefits, keeps inequality from hardening into a class system. Some point to the Great Gatsby Curve as support.

To represent this side fairly, state it in its strongest form, as its best defenders would. Do not pick its weakest supporter or its worst slogan. Then note its record. The democratic left built much of Europe's welfare states. The far left, in its revolutionary Communist form, also produced the Soviet Gulag and the Great Leap Forward famine in China. Most *social democrats* reject that path and support elections and markets with a strong safety net.

words.d: a broad political direction that tends to favor more equality and a larger role for government in reducing it
moving income or wealth from richer to poorer people through taxes and public programs
people on the democratic left who support elections and markets along with a strong welfare state

look.title: Strong Form or Weak Form?
look.text: Version A: The left just wants to take your money. Version B: Many on the left argue that public schools, health care and family support give poor children a fairer start, and they point to high mobility in Nordic countries as evidence.
look.prompt: Which version represents the left in its strongest form, and why would using the weaker version hurt your own argument?

check.q: What is redistribution?
choices: Moving income from richer to poorer people through taxes and programs
check.why: Redistribution uses taxes and benefits to move income toward poorer people.

check.q: Which countries do many on the left point to as evidence?
choices: The Nordic countries such as Denmark and Norway
check.why: They point to the Nordic mix of high taxes, strong public services and high mobility.

check.q: How do most social democrats differ from revolutionary Communists?
choices: They support elections and markets with a strong safety net
check.why: Social democrats work through elections and accept markets, unlike revolutionary Communist regimes.

lessons.title: The Strongest Case From the Right
lessons.mainIdea: Thinkers on the right often argue that opportunity grows from economic growth, strong families and communities, and personal responsibility.
reading: Many on the political *right* start from a different set of cases. South Korea was one of the poorest countries on Earth in the 1950s. Through fast growth driven by exports, hard work and heavy investment in education, it became a rich country within two generations. To right-leaning thinkers, *economic growth* is the most powerful ladder, because it creates jobs and lifts whole societies.

They also point to institutions outside government. Research by Raj Chetty and colleagues found that upward mobility was higher in American areas with more two-parent families, stronger community ties and more civic groups. Conservatives read this as support for strengthening families, churches and local communities. Many on the right also stress personal responsibility and *free markets*, arguing that high taxes and heavy rules can slow growth and discourage work.

Represent this side in its strongest form too, not by its worst slogan. Then note its record. The democratic right built much of the postwar prosperity in West Germany and Japan. The far right, in its Fascist and Nazi forms, produced violent dictatorships, war and the Holocaust. Mainstream *conservatives* reject that path and defend elections, the rule of law and individual rights.

words.d: a broad political direction that tends to favor tradition, free markets and a more limited role for government
an increase in the total amount of goods and services a country produces
an economy in which prices, jobs and businesses are shaped mostly by buyers and sellers rather than government
people on the democratic right who value tradition, stability and gradual change within the law

look.title: Two Readings of One Study
look.text: Chetty's team found that areas with higher upward mobility tended to have less residential segregation, less income inequality, better schools, more two-parent families and stronger community ties. A left-leaning writer highlights inequality and schools. A right-leaning writer highlights families and community.
look.prompt: Both writers cite the same study. What does that tell you about using evidence fairly, and how would you report the study in your own argument?

check.q: Why do many on the right point to South Korea?
choices: It had the world's largest welfare state
It became rich through fast growth driven by exports, work and education
check.why: South Korea's rapid growth from poverty is the right's example of growth as a ladder.

check.q: Which finding from Chetty's research do conservatives stress?
choices: Higher mobility in areas with more two-parent families and stronger community ties
Lower mobility wherever taxes were low
Higher mobility only in the largest cities
check.why: They read the family and community findings as support for strengthening those institutions.

check.q: How do mainstream conservatives differ from Fascists?
choices: They defend elections, the rule of law and individual rights
check.why: Mainstream conservatives work within democracy, unlike Fascist and Nazi regimes.

lessons.title: Knowing the Other Side
lessons.mainIdea: You understand your own position only when you can state the strongest opposing case as well as its supporters can.
reading: In 1859 the English philosopher John Stuart Mill wrote On Liberty. He argued that a person who has only heard one side of a question does not truly understand even their own view. You need to hear opposing arguments from people who actually believe them, at their most persuasive. Only then can you know why your view holds up, if it does.

Today people call this *steelmanning*: building the strongest version of an argument you disagree with. It is the opposite of a *straw man*, a weak, twisted version of the other side that is easy to knock down. A straw man may win applause from people who already agree. It will not convince anyone else, and it leaves your own thinking untested.

A simple test helps. Could a supporter of the other side read your summary of their view and say, Yes, that is what I believe? If so, you have been fair. Watch also for *confirmation bias*, the habit of noticing evidence that fits what you already think and skipping what does not. Maya's early plan to find three studies that agreed with her was confirmation bias at work.

words.d: stating the strongest, fairest version of an argument you disagree with
a weak or twisted version of someone's argument, made so it is easy to attack
the habit of favoring evidence that supports what you already believe

look.title: John Stuart Mill on Hearing Both Sides
look.text: He who knows only his own side of the case, knows little of that.
look.cite: John Stuart Mill, On Liberty, chapter 2, 1859
look.prompt: Explain Mill's sentence in your own words. How would following it change the way you research your capstone question?

check.q: What is a straw man?
choices: The strongest version of an opposing view
A weak or twisted version of someone's argument, easy to attack
check.why: A straw man misrepresents the other side so it is easy to knock down.

check.q: What did Mill argue in On Liberty?
choices: A person who knows only their own side barely understands it
Arguments should be settled by majority vote
check.why: Mill wrote that knowing only your own side means knowing little of it.

check.q: Maya planned to find only studies that agreed with her. What is this called?
check.why: Confirmation bias is favoring evidence that fits what you already believe.

lessons.title: Claim, Evidence and Reasoning
lessons.mainIdea: A strong argument states a clear claim, supports it with specific evidence and explains the reasoning that links the two.
reading: Here is a claim Maya might write: Access to paid, recognized job training outside university helps many young people move up. Her evidence: Germany's dual system reaches a large share of young people, and Germany's youth unemployment has stayed lower than many European neighbors'. Her *reasoning*: a paid path with a recognized credential lets students earn while learning, so family money matters less.

In 1958 the British philosopher Stephen Toulmin described the parts of an everyday argument. The *claim* is what you want the reader to accept. The data or *evidence* are the facts that support it. The warrant is the reasoning that explains why the evidence supports the claim. Many classrooms now teach this as claim, evidence and reasoning.

Strong writers also add a *qualifier*, a word that shows how sure they are, such as often, in many cases or probably. Maya's claim says many young people, not all. Qualifiers are not weakness. They are honesty about what the evidence can carry. A claim that is too strong breaks when a reader finds one exception.

words.d: the main point an argument asks the reader to accept
facts, data or sources that support a claim
the explanation of why the evidence supports the claim; Toulmin called it the warrant
a word or phrase, such as often or probably, that shows how strongly a claim is made

look.title: The Parts of an Argument
look.text: An everyday argument moves from data to a claim. What lets us make that step is a warrant, a general rule that links the two. A careful arguer also says how strongly the claim holds, and under what conditions it might not.
look.cite: Stephen Toulmin, The Uses of Argument, 1958 (paraphrased)
look.prompt: In Maya's argument about apprenticeships, identify the claim, the data and the warrant.

check.q: In Toulmin's model, what is the warrant?
choices: The main point you want accepted
The reasoning that explains why the evidence supports the claim
check.why: The warrant is the link between evidence and claim, taught today as reasoning.

check.q: Which word in a claim is a qualifier?
check.why: Often shows how strongly the claim is made, which is what a qualifier does.

check.q: Why does the reading say qualifiers make an argument stronger?
choices: They show honesty about what the evidence can support
They remove the need for sources
check.why: A claim that is too strong breaks at one exception; a qualified claim matches the evidence.

lessons.title: Answering Counterarguments
lessons.mainIdea: A strong argument names the best objection to its claim and answers it honestly, by rebutting it, limiting the claim or conceding the point.
reading: A reader of Maya's argument might object: Germany sorts students into school tracks at about age ten, so apprenticeships may lock working-class children out of university. This is a *counterargument*, a reason someone might reject your claim. It is a serious one, raised by German researchers themselves. Ignoring it would make Maya's essay weaker.

There are three honest ways to answer. You can offer a *rebuttal*, evidence that the objection is wrong or smaller than it seems. For example, Germany offers routes from vocational training to later university study. You can narrow your claim so it no longer overreaches. Or you can make a *concession*, admitting the objection has force, and then explain why your claim still holds on balance.

Place the counterargument where a reader would raise it, often after your main evidence. State it fairly, in its strongest form. Answer it with evidence, not with a label or an insult. Readers trust writers who show them the whole field. A capstone that answers the best objection is more persuasive, not less, because the reader can see the claim has been tested.

words.d: a reason or piece of evidence that someone might use to reject your claim
a response showing that a counterargument is wrong or less important than it seems
admitting that part of an opposing argument is true while explaining why your claim still holds

look.title: Three Ways to Answer
look.text: Claim: Conditional cash transfers like Mexico's Progresa help poor children move up. Objection: Paying families might make them depend on government. Response 1: That is a silly worry. Response 2: Studies of Progresa found higher school enrollment, and the payments were tied to school attendance. Response 3: Dependence is a fair concern, so programs should be judged over the long run.
look.prompt: Which response is a rebuttal, which is a concession, and which one should a strong writer never use? Explain.

check.q: What is a counterargument?
choices: A reason someone might reject your claim
check.why: A counterargument is an objection to your claim.

check.q: What is a concession?
choices: Admitting part of an objection is true while explaining why your claim still holds
check.why: A concession grants the objection some force but keeps the claim on balance.

check.q: Why does answering the best objection make an argument more persuasive?
choices: It proves the other side has no evidence
Readers can see the claim has been tested
It avoids the need for a claim
check.why: Readers trust a writer who shows the whole field and tests the claim against it.

lessons.title: Presenting and Discussing Respectfully
lessons.mainIdea: Sharing your argument well means speaking clearly, listening fully and disagreeing with ideas without attacking people.
reading: Maya presents her findings to her class. A classmate, Andre, disagrees: he thinks college is still the surest road up in the United States. Maya does not roll her eyes. She says, Tell me more about your evidence. Andre cites data showing college graduates earn more on average. Maya agrees that the pattern is real, then shares her German and Danish comparisons. Both leave with something new.

This is *civil discourse*: discussion in which people disagree honestly while treating each other with respect. A few habits make it work. Listen to understand, not only to reply. Restate the other person's point before you answer it. Critique the idea, never the person. An *ad hominem* attack, aimed at a person instead of their argument, proves nothing about the argument.

When you present, make it easy to follow. Start with your question and claim. Show two or three pieces of evidence, each with its source named. Give the strongest counterargument and your answer. End with what you still do not know. Visual aids help many listeners. A clear chart or map with a *citation* on it lets your audience check your evidence for themselves.

words.d: honest discussion in which people disagree while treating each other with respect
an attack on a person instead of on their argument
a note naming the author or body, title and year of a source so others can find it

look.title: Two Replies
look.text: A classmate says democracies last mainly because countries are wealthy. Reply A: You only think that because you never read anything. Reply B: So you are saying wealth is the main factor. That fits Przeworski's finding, but how would you explain India, which kept its democracy while still poor?
look.prompt: Which reply practices civil discourse? Name two habits from the reading that it uses.

check.q: What is an ad hominem attack?
choices: An attack on a person instead of their argument
check.why: Ad hominem targets the person, which proves nothing about the argument.

check.q: What did Maya do when Andre disagreed?
choices: She asked about his evidence and acknowledged what was true in it
check.why: She listened, asked for his evidence, agreed the pattern was real and then shared her own.

check.q: Which step belongs at the end of a strong presentation, according to the reading?
choices: Repeating your claim with no evidence
Saying what you still do not know
check.why: The reading says to end with what you still do not know, which is honest about the limits of evidence.

review.q: Which makes the strongest capstone question?
choices: Why did Chile's democracy fall in 1973 while Costa Rica's survived?
How can we fix every problem at once?
review.why: It is open, arguable, researchable and narrow enough to finish.

choices: Stating the strongest, fairest version of a view you disagree with
review.why: Steelmanning represents the other side as its best defenders would.

review.q: What does the Great Gatsby Curve show?
choices: That college always leads to wealth
That countries with more inequality tend to have less mobility
review.why: It is a correlation between inequality and lower mobility across countries.

review.q: Levitsky and Ziblatt argue democracies depend on unwritten norms. Which is one of them?
review.why: Mutual toleration and forbearance are their two key guardrails.

review.q: How do the left and right usually differ on what helps people move up?
choices: The left stresses public investment and less inequality; the right stresses growth, families and markets
The left opposes schools; the right opposes jobs
review.why: Each side emphasizes different causes, and each cites real evidence.

review.q: Which pair names extreme records from both the far left and the far right?
choices: Obon and the Day of the Dead
The Khmer Rouge killings and the Holocaust
The Basic Law and On Liberty
review.why: The Khmer Rouge was a Communist regime and the Holocaust was carried out by the Nazi regime.

review.q: In claim, evidence and reasoning, what does the reasoning do?
choices: Explains why the evidence supports the claim
review.why: Reasoning, Toulmin's warrant, links the evidence to the claim.

review.q: Why should you gather evidence from at least two regions?
choices: To test whether a pattern is general or local
Because one region has no data
To make the claim stronger than the evidence
review.why: Comparative analysis shows whether a cause seems to matter beyond one place.
